_about: Your project's own notes and decisions. The Knowledge base tab reads this file at runtime. Add an entry whenever you decide something or learn a limit; the platform never writes this file.

entries.title: plan.json is left exactly as the platform wrote it
entries.body: The platform stops refreshing plan.json once it is edited by hand. The published plan has gaps (no requirements, placeholder dates), so instead of patching it, every tab shows an honest empty state and Overview > Plan check lists the gaps. The tabs fill in on their own when the plan is republished.

entries.title: Static site with hash routes, entry point at the repo root
entries.body: index.html sits at the root so GitHub Pages can serve it; every tab and every detail page is its own #/ address. There is no build step. A .nojekyll file makes Pages serve the .colaberry/ folder the page reads.

entries.title: All data reaches the tabs through one module
entries.body: data.js loads plan.json, progress.json and manifest.json (or the sample files) and joins them on story id. Tabs only read that model, so pointing the page at the running system later changes one file.

entries.title: This page cannot check any connection
entries.body: A static page cannot reach other systems or hold a secret. Every system status is grey and 'not checked from here' until the running system reports its own connections.

entries.title: The chat panel is a lookup, not a language model
entries.body: It answers questions about stories, releases, dates, requirements, guardrails, systems, measures, roles, owners and data age from the files on this page, cites the tab, and says so when the files do not hold the answer.

entries.title: STORY-001 runs against a stand-in GIS until the city GIS is connected
entries.body: There is no access to Herriman's GIS database yet (no URL, account or credentials). Work orders talk to GIS only through createGisClient(), which adds a timeout and capped retries; behind it is a stand-in with made-up assets. A real GIS adapter needs the same two methods (getAsset, linkWorkOrder). STORY-001's GIS criteria were verified against the stand-in, not the city's GIS.

entries.title: Every work order change and its audit entry are saved in one transaction
entries.body: Create, update and complete each write their audit entry inside the same database transaction as the change, so a change can never exist without its audit record. If the audit write fails, the change is rolled back. GIS write-back happens after the save and is queued, so a GIS outage never loses a work order.

entries.title: GIS changes reach work orders by polling, not webhooks
entries.body: processGisChanges() asks GIS for numbered changes after the last one processed and remembers its place in gis_cursor. Polling needs nothing set up on the city's side and is safe to run again; webhooks would need the city GIS to call us. Nothing runs it on a schedule yet.

entries.title: GIS owns asset data; the work order system owns work order fields
entries.body: A GIS change can update a work order's asset snapshot, address and coordinates, never its title, priority or status. The two sides never write the same field, so there is no conflict to resolve. Completed work orders are not changed by GIS; the skip is reported.

entries.title: The GIS credential comes only from the GIS_TOKEN environment variable
entries.body: It is passed to GIS on every call and never written to the repo, the logs or a commit. A refused credential is not retried, because retrying a bad password does not help and can lock the account.

entries.title: Madison AI gets an audited API, not direct database access
entries.body: REQ-040 allows open database or API compatibility. An API was chosen because direct database reads could not be logged per access, and the Trust criterion requires every Madison AI data access in the audit trail. The API is read-only: list, changes since a time, search and get one.

entries.title: No audit entry, no data
entries.body: Every API read and its audit entry run in one transaction. If the audit entry cannot be written, the request is refused with 503 and nothing is returned. Refused keys are audited too, without recording the key.

entries.title: One fixed, versioned data format for outside systems
entries.body: Work orders leave the system only through toPublic(), in schema version 1. The OpenAPI contract and the format checker are generated from the same field list, so the published contract cannot drift from the real responses. Internal fields (request_id, sync queues, the audit trail) are never exposed.

entries.title: Madison AI's own requirements are not known yet
entries.body: The API was proven against our published contract and a simulated crawler. Madison AI's real spec, authentication method and credentials still need to be obtained and checked against it.

entries.title: A locate ticket cannot be closed until the one-call centre has its final answer
entries.body: Completing a ticket is refused if it has no response, if the response has not been delivered to the one-call centre, or if the last response asked for more time. Completed tickets are locked against further updates and responses.

entries.title: Ticket responses are queued, resent and never delivered twice
entries.body: A response is saved, audited and placed in bluestakes_outbox in one transaction, then sent with a timeout and capped retries; every attempt is logged in bluestakes_log. If the centre is down the response stays pending for deliverPendingResponses(). Each response has a response_id so a resend cannot be stored twice.

entries.title: Changing locate tickets needs its own API permission
entries.body: Ticket endpoints need an API key with locate_tickets:write. A read-only key (such as Madison AI's) gets 403, no key gets 401, and every refusal is audited. Each change records the person and the calling system, e.g. 'locator-1 via City app'. Per-person logins arrive with STORY-007.

entries.title: Blue Stakes is a stand-in and the response codes are placeholders
entries.body: Tickets come from server/bluestakes/stand-in-tickets.json in an assumed format, and the response codes (marked, clear_no_conflict, needs_more_time) are placeholders. Both need replacing with Blue Stakes of Utah's real feed format and official codes once the city has access.

entries.title: Citizen requests are private until staff publish them
entries.body: Every public submission becomes a work order, but it is not shown to the public until staff publish it (publishWorkOrder, audited). The citizen can always follow their own request with its tracking code. The public view shows status and a plain-language history, never staff names, notes, contact details or IPs.

entries.title: A hidden work order looks exactly like a missing one
entries.body: Asking the public site for an unpublished work order returns the same 404 and message as one that does not exist, so nobody can probe for hidden records.

entries.title: Submission IPs come from the connection and stay in a staff-only log
entries.body: The IP is the network connection's own address; X-Forwarded-For is used only when the server is configured to sit behind a trusted proxy. IPs are stored only in public_submission_log, which no public or outside-system endpoint returns. Every attempt is logged, including invalid, unreadable and rate-limited ones.

entries.title: IP retention is a 90-day placeholder
entries.body: purgeSubmissionIps() clears IPs older than 90 days but nothing runs it on a schedule, and 90 days is a placeholder until the city's records retention rule is known.

entries.title: Spam limit on public reports
entries.body: One address can have at most 5 accepted reports per hour; the next gets 429 and is logged as rate_limited. The limit is in one place (RATE_LIMIT).

entries.title: Outside systems change work orders with ETag / If-Match versioning
entries.body: Every work order has a version that goes up on every change. Outside systems get it as an ETag and must send it back as If-Match to update or complete: a stale version gets 412 with the current work order, a missing one gets 428. This stops a system overwriting a change it has not seen. The version is a header, so Madison AI's published format (schema_version 1) did not change.

entries.title: Safe retries with an Idempotency-Key, scoped to each system
entries.body: A create sent again with the same Idempotency-Key returns the first work order (200, Idempotent-Replayed: true). Keys are combined with the calling system's id, so two systems can never collide on the same key.

entries.title: Every API request is logged; bodies as field names only
entries.body: api_request_log gets one row for every request to the server, whatever the endpoint or outcome: times, method, path, query, client, IP, status, error code, and the body's field names and size. Body values and API keys are never stored, because bodies can carry personal data. Each response carries an X-Request-Id to quote when reporting a problem.

entries.title: The published contract and the request checks come from one list
entries.body: The write endpoints check bodies against BODIES, and the OpenAPI request bodies are generated from the same object, so the specification an outside system reads is exactly what the API enforces. Responses are checked against the published format before they are sent.

entries.title: API specifications still need coordinating with the actual vendors
entries.body: REQ-054 asks for API specifications and testing to be coordinated with specific vendors. The API and its contract exist and were tested with a simulated system, but no vendor has reviewed or tested against them yet. That is work for people, planned with STORY-009.

entries.title: A vendor submission is confirmed stored before its receipt is sent
entries.body: The answer, its documents and its audit entry are saved together, then read back and checked against a SHA-256 fingerprint inside the same transaction. A mismatch rolls everything back and tells the vendor to submit again. The receipt carries the fingerprints as proof of what was received.

entries.title: Every vendor submission received is audited, even if nothing is stored
entries.body: Stored submissions are audited as submit; repeats of a submission_key as submit_duplicate; refused ones (invalid data, a disguised file, one already waiting for review) as submit_rejected with the reasons.

entries.title: Documents are accepted for what they are, not what they are called
entries.body: Only PDF, Word .docx and plain text, at most 5 per submission and 5 MB each. The first bytes must match the declared type, the file name extension must match, and names are cleaned of paths. Downloads are always sent as attachments under a sandboxing policy, so an uploaded file cannot run as a page.

entries.title: Reviewers approve or request changes; vendors are kept apart
entries.body: A reviewer cannot review a submission from their own organisation, and requesting changes needs a comment. Vendors see only their own submissions: another vendor's looks exactly like a missing one. Resubmitting after changes requested creates a new revision and keeps the old one.

entries.title: The requirements catalog is copied from the brief, and the overdue limit is a placeholder
entries.body: plan.json has no requirements, so server/vendor/requirements.json holds the 18 from the STORY-000 brief; a test keeps its ids in step with the plan's stories. Reviews waiting over 5 days are flagged overdue — a placeholder until the city sets a review deadline. The portal is API endpoints only; there is no vendor web page yet.

entries.title: Heat maps count unmapped work orders instead of hiding them
entries.body: A work order is placed by its own coordinates (from GIS) or the map pin a citizen gave. Work orders with only a freeform location cannot be placed; they are counted as unmapped, and every map says how many. Cell counts plus unmapped always equal the work orders matching the filters. There is no automatic address lookup, which would need an outside geocoding service.

entries.title: One fixed grid; GeoJSON for a street-map view in the city GIS
entries.body: Cells are squares on a grid fixed at Herriman's latitude, so maps from different runs line up. The SVG image has no street map (that needs an outside tile service); the GeoJSON output loads into the city's GIS on top of one.

entries.title: Heat maps are staff-only and contain counts, never individual work orders
entries.body: GET /api/v1/heat-maps needs heatmaps:read. A cell holding one work order can point to one citizen's report, so heat maps are never public, and only per-cell counts and type breakdowns are returned.

entries.title: Every heat map generation is logged — no log, no map
entries.body: heat_map_log gets a row for every generation attempt: ok, invalid (bad parameters) or failed (too detailed, drawing failed, data unreadable), with who, parameters, times and counts. If the row cannot be written, the map is not returned. Maps over 5,000 cells or 250,000 grid squares are refused with advice to use larger cells.

entries.title: Grid heat maps split neighbours at cell edges
entries.body: Two work orders a few metres apart can fall either side of a cell boundary and be counted in different cells. This is inherent to a fixed grid; a smoothed (kernel density) map would avoid it but was not needed for REQ-031.
entries.evidence: tests/heatMaps.test.js (a larger cell size merges nearby points)
